newsitem.title: UK: UK "wise people" to call for only modest tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: UK "wise people" to call for only modest tax cuts.

text.p: Most of the British Treasury's independent economic advisers believe Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has room for no more than modest tax cuts in his last pre-election budget next month.

And all but one of the six panel members known as the "wise people" will call for no further cuts in interest rates, although most expect no increase before the elections, which must be held by May 1997.
Clarke will unveil his budget on November 26 and the "wise people" will publish their pre-budget submission on Friday.
The following comments from all six of the independent advisers are taken from interviews with Reuters or from recent statements and publications.
MARTIN WEALE, RESEARCH DIRECTOR AT THE NATIONAL INSTITUTE FOR ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL RESEARCH:

Weale said prudence dictates that Clarke should not cut taxes at all this year. He argues that increases of up to 3.0 billion pounds, together with curbs on public spending, would be wiser to put the public finances on a sound footing.
He said the chances of underlying UK inflation hitting its 2.5 percent target next year were now less than 50 percent.

Nevertheless, the latest NIESR economic review assumes that the basic rate of income tax will be cut by one penny in the pound to 23 percent and that personal tax allowances will be increased by more than the rate of inflation.
That would cost about 4.0 billion pounds.
The NIESR report said some monetary tightening was needed to improve the chances of the inflation target being met, but said it was possible Clarke could avoid a pre-election rate rise.
GAVYN DAVIES, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT GOLDMAN SACHS:

In its "Green Budget", produced with the Institute for Fiscal Studies three weeks ago, Goldman Sachs said Clarke could cut taxes modestly, by around 3.0 billion pounds, paid for by cuts in planned spending in the following fiscal year.
But it said tax cuts may prove unwise if the government intends to meet planned reductions in public borrowing in the medium term.
Goldman Sachs does not expect official interest rates, now at 5.75 percent, to be changed before general elections which must be held by May 1997.
TIM CONGDON, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT LOMBARD STREET RESEARCH:
Congdon told Reuters he thought Britain's budget position was not sustainable. "There should still be efforts to reduce the budget deficit. Any tax cuts should at least be matched by spending cuts."
But he expects Clarke to make net tax cuts of around two billion pounds.

Two weeks ago Congdon, a strict monetarist, called for an immediate one percentage point increase in interest rates, arguing that this would avert the need for more drastic action later on. He said the British economy was enjoying a mini-boom.
PATRICK MINFORD, LIVERPOOL UNIVERSITY
Minford remains a lone voice on the UK Treasury panel with his argument that monetary policy is too tight and that interest rates should be cut to 5.25 percent.
"I think the economy is still recovering and any rise in interest rates would be premature," he told Reuters.
Minford favours swingeing tax cuts, arguing that the government's budget deficit forecasts are perfectly plausible and that the welfare state could be pruned after the election.
"They could cut taxes by as much as 12 billion pounds on that basis, although of course they won't. But they can afford at least four billion," Minford told Reuters.
"I would like to see two pence off the basic rate of income tax at this budget and promises of a rolling programme of tax cuts, based on the ongoing control of public spending."
BRIDGET ROSEWELL, JOINT MANAGING DIRECTOR, BUSINESS STRATEGIES LTD:

Rosewell told Reuters she would like to see a neutral-to-tight budget, with any tax cuts at least balanced by spending cuts. "That really means steady as she goes," she said. "I'd like to see very little changed in this budget."

She took a similar line on monetary policy, saying sterling's recent rise meant any extra monetary tightening was unnecessary for the time being. The pound has gained more than six percent on a trade-weighted basis since early August.
"Clarke can probably get away with it until after the election as things stand," she said.
KATE BARKER, CHIEF ECONOMIC ADVISER AT THE CONFEDERATION OF BRITISH INDUSTRY:

The CBI's view on monetary and fiscal policy is well known -- rates should not be cut further. Last week, it said Clarke "might get away" with leaving interest rates on hold until the election, but it certainly saw no scope for easier credit.

In its recent budget presentation, the CBI urged the government to trim its real spending target by about two billion pounds and cut taxes by only about one billion -- a net fiscal tightening. But it conceded that tax cuts of three billion pounds or more were likely.
